title: The Wartburg
hookLine: hidden in a castle, Luther translates the New Testament into everyday German

lines: A KIDNAPPING THAT WAS A RESCUE.
cards: A wagon on a forest road, heading home from Worms. Horsemen burst out of the trees, drag one passenger out, and gallop off with him. Word spreads that Luther has been seized, maybe killed.
In fact the kidnapping is a rescue, arranged by his own prince to hide him. That night he's taken up to a castle on a hill, the Wartburg. His monk's habit is gone.
He lets his hair and beard grow, and the castle staff call him Knight George. And there, an outlaw now, he picks up the Greek New Testament.

teach.b: Luther worked from the Greek text Erasmus had printed, the one from a few days ago.
He set out to put it into German: not German bent into the shape of the Latin, word for word, but German the way people actually spoke it. In a letter defending his translation, he explained how.
You don't ask the Latin letters how to speak German, he wrote.

teach.h: ASK THE MOTHER IN THE HOUSE.
teach.b: You ask the mother in the house, the children in the street, the common man in the market, and you watch their mouths as they talk. Then you translate that way, and they'll understand you. He even gave an example.
In the King James Bible, Jesus says: "for out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh." Put word for word into German, Luther said, that sounds like nobody's mother talking.
A German mother would say something closer to: when the heart is full, the mouth runs over. So that's what he wrote. Not every scholar liked it.
Some said he bent the text, and Luther pushed back hard. There's also an old story that he threw his inkwell at the devil in that room. It may well be a legend.
What isn't legend is the result: a New Testament in German that could be read aloud at home, in the language of the market. And the work didn't belong only to Protestants.
Catholic scholars produced German Bibles too, and in English, translators like Tyndale were doing the same thing, chasing the words of ordinary speech.

how: Christians across churches read the Bible in their own languages today, and Bible translators still face Luther's question of how close to stay to the original wording and how close to ordinary speech.

practice: Choose one thing you know well that other people find confusing, your job, the rules of a game, a line of scripture, and explain it in your head in the words you'd use with a child at the kitchen table.
If a word sounds like a document, swap it for one that sounds like a person, until the whole thing sounds like talk. If you pray, offer that plain explanation as a gift.

wordCard.voice: The Wartburg. The castle where Luther hid as Knight George and turned the Greek New Testament into the everyday German of the house, the street and the market.

carryVoice: Your line: the language of the market. Plain words can carry deep things. See you soon.
